newsitem.title: UK: EBRD-FORMER SOVIET BLOC GETS TICKING OFF FROM WEST.
newsitem.headline: EBRD-FORMER SOVIET BLOC GETS TICKING OFF FROM WEST.

text.p: Former Soviet bloc countries, used to being handled with kid gloves by western governments, received an unexpected ticking off at the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
U.S. Treasury official David Lipton said the transition to market economies in the region, which the EBRD was set up in 1991 to promote, was "moving ahead with momentum".
But he and other top western bankers and officials warned on Monday that crime and corruption could torpedo reform drives by countries in eastern and central Europe.
"We are concerned that across the region crime and corruption could undermine reform. We are calling on countries to crack down on criminality," Lipton told Reuters in an interview.

Some officials said the unusually critical tone of western comments was a sign of the comparative maturity of the new reform states -- in previous years, westerners would have been wary of destabilising them by making harsh comments.
EBRD President Jacques de Larosiere listed legal uncertainties, taxation systems and corruption as major obstacles deterring foreign investors.
"There is corruption, crime and the arbitrary interference of some officials in private sector business activities," he said.
A senior New Zealand official said no one would pretend that economic reform was an easy road to tread.
"It is tempting to sit down for a rest," said Peter Bennett, head of the foreign ministry's European office.
"But...commitment to reform is essential to macroeconomic stabilisation and sustained growth in the Bank's countries of operation."

The former communist bloc is divided into countries like Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, which are well on the road to reform, and those like Belarus, Bulgaria and Romania which still have much to do.

"The time has come for those who are lagging behind to pull ahead with wider and deeper reforms, so as to share in the economic revival that the best reformers are currently experiencing," Italian Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said.
The EBRD has been shifting its focus towards Russia and former Soviet republics, where reform is at an early stage.
Lipton said many of these countries now recognised that the battle against corruption, often at the highest levels of government, was an urgent priority.
"They are becoming focused on the fact that there are lots of potential investors out there and they want the money to start flowing. So there is now a healthy pragmatism," he said.
German finance ministry state secretary Juergen Stark said the EBRD should scale down its activities in the most successful countries in favour of the weaker ones.

"The Bank must begin to withdraw from operations in the advanced central European countries, for which an increasing volume of private finance is on hand. It must not substitute private capital flows," he said.
But Lipton and Larosiere said no country was yet at the stage where the EBRD could pull out altogether.
"The Bank's policy is to follow countries down the transition path, milestone by milestone, not simply to pull out completely once a certain stage is reached," Lipton added.
